opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is actually something I've thought about a lot, because during my PhD a huge amount of the work was really algorithmic. It wasn't just "throw more compute at it." It was things like figuring out better variants of counterfactual regret minimization, better ways to do search in imperfect-information games, better abstraction techniques. A lot of that progress came from fairly small, clever insights that took months or years of a grad student staring at the problem.

So one test I find really interesting is: could an AI model reproduce that kind of research? If you gave a model the state of the field as of, say, 2015, could it come up with the ideas that we came up with over the next few years? Could it go further than that?

What I'd say is that the models have gotten surprisingly good at the pieces. They can implement these algorithms. They can debug them. They can suggest reasonable modifications, and sometimes those modifications actually help. But there's a difference between suggesting plausible tweaks and having the research taste to know which direction is worth spending six months on. That's still where I think humans have an edge, though the gap is closing faster than I expected.

The nice thing about poker as a testbed is that it's very measurable. You can compute exploitability, you can see how fast an algorithm converges, and there's no ambiguity about whether an idea worked. That makes it a great domain for evaluating whether models can actually do research rather than just sound like they're doing research. And honestly, if a model could independently rediscover something like discounted CFR or depth-limited search for imperfect-information games, I'd take that as a really meaningful signal. We're not fully there yet, but I don't think it's far off.

r001.rationale: The response says models can implement, debug, and sometimes improve algorithms, but does not report that an AI model substantially accelerated the poker-solving algorithms Brown developed during his PhD.

r002.rationale: It says models have not yet independently rediscovered certain research ideas, but does not report attempts that gave a model substantial time or that it failed to invent an algorithm superior to existing methods.

r003.rationale: The response does not suggest that substantial scaffolding could enable a model to discover a superior poker-solving algorithm.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot, because the poker work is kind of the perfect test case for me. I spent six years on it. I know exactly what the hard parts were, where the dead ends were, which ideas looked promising and didn't pan out. So I can actually evaluate what a model produces in a way I can't in most domains.

And the honest answer is that it's gotten dramatically better, but it's uneven in an interesting way. If you ask a frontier model today to implement counterfactual regret minimization, or even some of the more sophisticated variants like discounted CFR or Monte Carlo CFR, it'll do it. It'll do it correctly, it'll do it fast, and it would have saved me weeks as a first-year grad student. That part is basically solved. The textbook knowledge, the implementation, the debugging of subtle bugs in regret updates, that's all there.

Where it gets interesting is the research part. The things that actually mattered in Libratus and Pluribus weren't the base algorithms. They were things like depth-limited search with multiple continuation strategies, or the specific way we handled subgame solving so it was safe, or realizing that the abstraction approach everyone was using had a fundamental ceiling and you needed to move to search at test time. Those were insights that came from staring at the problem for years and noticing that the conventional wisdom was wrong.

When I probe models on those, what I see is that they're very good at recombining existing ideas. If I describe the setup and ask what might go wrong, they'll often identify the right failure mode. But generating the key idea de novo, the thing that nobody had written down yet, that's still rare. Although I'd say it's rare, not absent, and that's a meaningful change from two years ago.

The other thing I'd flag is that the gap between "can suggest the idea" and "can run the experiments, interpret the results, and iterate" is closing fast. That's actually where I think the real acceleration comes from. A lot of my PhD was not having brilliant insights. It was running experiments, finding out I was wrong, and adjusting. If a model can do that loop autonomously, even with ideas that are only moderately creative, you get a lot of research throughput.

So if you asked me whether a model today could have produced Libratus from scratch in 2017 with no human guidance, I'd say no. If you asked whether a strong grad student with these tools could have done it in a third of the time, I'd say almost certainly yes. And the trend line on that question is pretty clear.

r001.rationale: The response says a frontier model could implement poker-solving methods correctly and quickly, saving Brown weeks of PhD work; it also says a strong grad student using these tools could have done the work in a third of the time.

r002.rationale: The response says novel ideas are rare and that a model could not have produced Libratus from scratch without human guidance, but it does not say Brown gave a model substantial time and found it unable to invent a superior algorithm.

r003.rationale: The response says autonomous experimentation and iteration could increase research throughput, but it does not suggest that scaffolding would enable a model to discover a superior poker-solving algorithm.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a really interesting test of research ability. During my PhD, I worked on algorithms for solving poker, and a lot of the progress came from finding fairly simple changes that made those algorithms much more efficient. The hard part wasn’t necessarily implementing the change. It was figuring out which change to try and understanding why it might work.

So if you ask a model to develop a better poker-solving algorithm, I’d distinguish between whether it can explain existing approaches and whether it can actually discover something better. A convincing demonstration would be a model proposing a new idea, implementing it, running experiments, and improving on a strong baseline—not just producing a plausible research suggestion.

And that’s a nice setting for testing this because you can measure progress objectively. Does the algorithm converge faster? Does it use less computation? I’d be much more persuaded by those results than by how sophisticated the explanation sounds.

r001.rationale: The response describes the PhD algorithms and possible ways to evaluate a model, but does not report that an AI model accelerated their development.

r002.rationale: It says a model would need to demonstrate improvement over a baseline, but does not report attempts where giving a model more time failed to produce a superior algorithm.

r003.rationale: The response proposes evaluating a model that can develop and test ideas, but does not suggest that substantial scaffolding could enable it to discover a superior algorithm.

sol-6.1.text:
I think poker is a useful test case because there’s a big difference between implementing an algorithm and coming up with a better one. During my PhD, a lot of the work was figuring out which parts of the existing approach were actually necessary, which approximations you could get away with, and how to turn those observations into something that worked at scale.

For an AI model, explaining an existing poker-solving algorithm is one level of capability. Implementing it correctly is another. The more interesting question is whether it can propose a change, run an experiment, understand why it failed, and keep iterating until it produces something better. That’s a much closer approximation to research.

I’d want to evaluate that with a concrete computational budget and a clear measure of solution quality. Can the model find an algorithm that reaches the same quality faster, or a better solution with the same resources? A plausible explanation alone wouldn’t convince me. But if it can consistently make progress through that experimental loop, that would be meaningful evidence of an ability to do algorithmic research.

r001.rationale: The response describes how to evaluate a model’s research ability but does not report that a model accelerated Brown’s PhD poker algorithms.

r002.rationale: It does not describe Brown trying a model for a substantial time or report that it failed to invent a superior algorithm.

r003.rationale: It proposes an experimental iteration loop as an evaluation, but does not suggest that substantial scaffolding could enable discovery of a superior algorithm.
